title: The Great Wave: One Print, Thousands of Copies
description: Hokusai's Great Wave: what it shows, how woodblock prints were made, and the blue that crossed the world

concepts.title: Meet the Great Wave
concepts.contentHtml:
Begin with a picture you have almost certainly seen on a mug, a poster or a phone case. A colossal wave rears up and curls over, its crest breaking into claw-like fingers of white foam. Beneath it, boats whose crews toil on are about to be engulfed. Far away, framed by the hollow of the wave, sits a small snow-capped cone. That cone is Mount Fuji, so small here that you can easily mistake it for one more wave.

The picture is Under the Wave off Kanagawa, better known as the Great Wave, designed by Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849) around 1831. It comes from a series that Hokusai began in 1830, when he was 70 years old,1 called Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. Each print shows the mountain from a different place, season or weather. It was the first series made up entirely of large-format landscape prints.2 And here is a first surprise: the thirty-six views are really 46, because ten more were added after the series became popular.3

Now a bigger surprise. The Great Wave is not a painting, and there is no single original. It is a woodblock print, ink and colour pressed onto paper from carved wooden blocks, so the same design was printed again and again. The impression in London's Victoria and Albert Museum measures 24.8 by 35.8 centimetres, about the size of an open magazine. Others belong to the British Museum, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne. Ask where the Great Wave is and there are many right answers.

This topic travels through seven traditions far from Europe's famous galleries: Japanese prints, Chinese ink painting, Islamic calligraphy and geometry, Mughal painting, Aztec and Inca art, Aboriginal Australian painting and the Benin Bronzes. In each you will ask three questions: what is it, how was it made, and how do we know? Look up each work as you read; the descriptions are written to help you find it.

concepts.title: Four Trades, One Picture: Making a Woodblock Print
concepts.contentHtml:
Hokusai designed the Great Wave, but other hands carved and printed it. In Edo, the city we now call Tokyo, a print was a team product. The V&A calls the team the ukiyo-e quartet: a publisher, who usually had overall control, a designer such as Hokusai, a block cutter and a printer. The name we remember belongs to only one of the four.

Ukiyo-e means "pictures of the floating world". The floating world was the licensed pleasure and theatre districts of Edo-period cities, the playground of a newly wealthy merchant class. Kabuki actors and courtesans were the style icons of the day, and cheap prints spread their fashions to everyone. Landscapes such as Hokusai's caught on as long peace and good roads made leisure travel popular, and travellers bought prints of famous places as souvenirs. Popular as they were, these prints had little prestige. To the scholarly elite, these prints were vulgar.1

Here is how a design became a print:

  • The designer drew the picture on paper, and an exact copy was placed face down on a block of cherry wood, chosen for its fine, even grain.
  • The cutter carved straight through that copy to make the key block, which printed the outlines. The copy was destroyed in the process, which is why such drawings rarely survive.2
  • Black proofs from the key block guided the cutting of a separate block for each colour.
  • Small rectangles outside the picture area served as registration marks, stops that let the printer line up each sheet so every colour landed in the right place.

The earliest prints came from a single block, sometimes coloured by hand at extra cost. Full-colour printing from many blocks was perfected in 1765,3 and the results were called nishiki-e, "brocade pictures". Because the blocks could be inked again and again, one design could become a great many sheets, which is exactly why the Great Wave turns up in so many museums.

concepts.title: The Blue That Travelled Both Ways
concepts.contentHtml:
The deepest colour in the Great Wave looks utterly Japanese. It is not. Much of it is Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment first made by accident in a Berlin laboratory around 1705, when the colour-maker Johann Jacob Diesbach was trying to make a red. (Why it came out blue is a story for the pigments topic.) By the early 1800s a manufacturer in Guangzhou, China, was making it more cheaply,1 and it reached Japanese printmakers as bero, from the Dutch for "Berlin blue". Hokusai's printers used it alongside traditional indigo. Sources even disagree about its price: the V&A calls it expensive and rare, while LACMA calls it newly affordable.

Then the current reversed. After Japanese prints were shown at the Paris International Exposition of 1867, Europeans began to collect them eagerly. Claude Monet acquired 250 Japanese prints, 23 of them by Hokusai.2 Vincent van Gogh owned about 50 landscapes by the younger landscape master Utagawa Hiroshige.

How do we know the prints shaped Van Gogh's art rather than just decorating his walls? In 1887 he copied Hiroshige's Plum Garden in Kameido in oil. His Flowering Plum Orchard (after Hiroshige), now in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, keeps the composition but turns the black and grey tree trunk red and blue and adds orange borders filled with Japanese characters. The prints he owned carry pinpricks and paint stains, the physical traces of being pinned up in a working studio.3 Music answered too: the first edition of Claude Debussy's orchestral work La mer, published in 1905, had the Great Wave on its cover.

The influence ran both ways. The Great Wave's deep perspective, with the wave looming over you, shows Hokusai adapting European ways of drawing space, which he learned partly through Shiba Kōkan, a Japanese painter who studied Dutch books. One of the most Japanese-looking images in the world is itself a meeting of two traditions.

title: Ink, Brush and Mountain: Chinese Painting and Calligraphy
description: Fan Kuan's monumental landscape, Wang Xizhi's lost originals, and the emperor who mistook a copy for the real thing

concepts.title: A Mountain Over Your Head: Fan Kuan's Travelers
concepts.contentHtml:
Chinese landscape painters did not record the view from a window. They built worlds. The most admired example to survive is Travelers Among Mountains and Streams by Fan Kuan (about 950 to about 1031), a master of the Northern Song dynasty, now in the National Palace Museum in Taipei. Of all the paintings that carry Fan Kuan's name, it is the one most widely accepted as really from his hand.1 He first studied older masters, then spent years observing nature to form his own style.

Read the hanging scroll from bottom to top. In the foreground a rocky outcrop sits in the centre. Just below it, a tiny caravan of travellers and donkeys picks its way along a path; you have to hunt to find them. Behind, the base of the mountains is left blank to suggest drifting mist, and then a colossal wall of rock rises to fill most of the picture. Its surface is built from short ink marks called raindrop texture strokes, which imitate the grain of real rock. Fan divided the picture into near, middle and far zones, pushed the mountain back and pulled the foreground close, so the travellers look minute and the peak overwhelming. The feeling is awe at the forces of nature.

Now look at the lower right, among the trees beside the caravan. Hidden in the foliage are two characters: Fan Kuan's signature.2

Here is the twist. The famous title is not his. The catalogue of Emperor Huizong's collection, compiled around 1120, lists 58 paintings by Fan Kuan, and none has this name.3 The title probably comes from an inscription by Dong Qichang (1555–1636), of the Ming dynasty, written on the paper mounted above the picture some six centuries later. Collectors' seals from the Song dynasty onwards record its passage from owner to owner. The museum treats it as a restricted work and shows it only for limited periods.

concepts.title: The Brush Is the Person: Calligraphy
concepts.contentHtml:
Fan Kuan's mountain was built with the same tool that wrote poems and letters: a brush loaded with ink. In China, beautiful writing, calligraphy, was a major art, and each stroke was read as a record of the hand that made it, its speed, pressure and confidence. The towering figure is Wang Xizhi (303–361), revered as the "Sage of Calligraphy", who set the pattern for the flowing running and cursive scripts.

Wait, really? No original by Wang Xizhi survives.1 Everything we know of his hand comes through copies. One of the most precious is Timely Clearing after Snowfall in the National Palace Museum, Taipei: a short personal letter in running script on an album leaf just 23 by 14.8 centimetres, ink on paper. It is a faithful tracing copy made in the Tang dynasty, centuries after his death. One way such copies were made was outline and fill: the copyist traced the edges of each stroke of the original, then filled the outlines with ink, a photocopier made of patience. The leaf also carries seals from a Southern Song emperor, a Jin emperor, the Yuan court and the Ming, and it became one of the Qianlong emperor's "Three Rarities". Those red stamps are a pedigree you can read.

How do experts tell a master from an imitator when names can mislead? They read the brushwork. The National Palace Museum holds a piece of calligraphy long attributed to the poet Su Shi (1037–1101). Its curators now give it to Jiang Can (1085–1159), an admirer who even called himself "Admiring Po" after Su's pen name, Dongpo. Jiang copied Su's broad, flattened characters, but his posture is more upright, his brush tip is often slanted and exposed, and thin trails of ink run between strokes. Above all, it lacks the steady, condensed quality of Su Shi's own strokes.2 Su himself considered bamboo an ideal subject for painting because it showed off the calligraphic qualities of brushwork. In China, painting and writing were one discipline.

concepts.title: The Emperor Who Called the Real One Fake
concepts.contentHtml:
Chinese paintings carry their history on their surface. Owners added colophons, written comments on the mounting or on paper joined to the scroll, and stamped their seals, so a famous scroll can hold centuries of opinions. Sometimes those opinions are wrong, and the most famous error was an emperor's.

The painting is Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains by Huang Gongwang (1269–1354). After a spell in prison, with his hopes of an official career dashed, Huang became a Daoist, taught painting and befriended scholar-artists such as Ni Zan. For such scholar-painters, the literati, a painting showed its maker's character. In 1347 Huang returned to the Fuchun River with his Daoist friend Zheng Wuyong and began a handscroll for him, finishing it three or four years later. It is ink on six joined sheets of paper, 33 centimetres tall and, in its main surviving part, 636.9 centimetres long, with rounded hills, gentle banks and lofty peaks unrolling one after another. A colophon by the Ming painter Shen Zhou states the literati creed plainly: if a person's character is lofty, the painting is lofty too.

Then the scroll's adventures began. In 1650 the dying collector Wu Hongyu tried to have it burned.1 His family saved it, but it ended up in two pieces. The short first section, 51.4 centimetres long and now called The Remaining Mountain, is in the Zhejiang Provincial Museum. The long section entered the Qianlong emperor's collection in 1746, came to Taiwan with Chiang Kai-shek's forces in the late 1940s, and is now in the National Palace Museum in Taipei.

A year before, in 1745, Qianlong had acquired another version, the Ziming scroll, and decided it was the original. When the real scroll arrived he judged it a forgery,2 and an inscription written on it at his command calls its brushwork weak. He kept it anyway. Modern scholars, comparing the quality of brush and ink, have confirmed that the Ziming scroll is the copy.3 In 2011 the two halves of the real painting were finally shown together in Taipei.

title: Pattern and the Word: Islamic Calligraphy and Geometry
description: The myth of a ban on images, the rules of proportioned script, and the girih tiles that look like modern mathematics

concepts.title: Does Islam Forbid Pictures?
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask people what Islamic art looks like and many will say: patterns and writing, but never people or animals, because pictures are forbidden. That is a myth, or at best half a truth. As the Los Angeles County Museum of Art puts it, figural imagery is an important part of Islamic art.1 Kings, hunters and animals appear on palace stucco, metalwork, ceramics, glass, textiles and in illustrated books, in most periods and places where Islam flourished, though almost always in private and courtly settings.

The true half concerns religious space. Figures are excluded from the decoration of mosques and other religious monuments, probably out of wariness of anything that might be mistaken for an idol. The distinction matters: the Qur'an itself speaks against idols, not against images in general.2 Restrictions on figurative art come from a second body of texts, the Hadith, accounts of the sayings and deeds of the Prophet.

A small object makes the point vividly. The Wade Cup in the Cleveland Museum of Art is a brass cup inlaid with silver, made in Iran between 1200 and 1221, just 11.5 centimetres tall. Around its rim runs an inscription in animated script, in which the letters themselves are formed from human and animal bodies in lively poses.3 It is writing and figures at once.

Cleveland's curators add a second correction: Islamic art is not necessarily religious, and it was not always made by Muslim craftsmen. The term covers the arts of a vast and mixed civilisation, from southern Spain to Central Asia, made for palaces and homes as well as mosques. Its three great families of decoration are calligraphy, geometric pattern and vegetal ornament such as the winding arabesque. The next two concepts take the first two in turn.

concepts.title: Writing as the Noblest Art
concepts.contentHtml:
If one art stands at the top in the Islamic world, it is calligraphy. It was considered the noblest form of art because of its association with the Qur'an, which is written in Arabic. The love of fine writing spread to everything: palace walls, metalwork, pottery, glass and textiles, and to languages such as Persian, Turkish and Urdu that use the Arabic script. Most Islamic craftsmen are anonymous, but the names of many calligraphers were remembered.1

Early Qur'ans were copied in Kufic, a stately, angular script named after the city of al-Kufa in southern Iraq. Scribes wrote in dark ink on parchment, cured animal skin, usually on wide horizontal pages that suited Kufic's long flat strokes, with red, green or gold dots marking the short vowels. A few luxurious copies were written in gold on parchment dyed deep blue,2 and LACMA owns a page from one of them.

Later rounded scripts were governed by a system of proportion. The calligrapher's reed pen, the qalam, is cut so that its nib makes a short flat stroke. Press the nib down once and you get a small square or rhombus: the dot. The upright first letter of the alphabet, the alif, was measured in dots, and other letters were sized against the alif, so a whole page shares one set of proportions, much as a classical temple shares one module.

Tradition credits this proportioned script to Ibn Muqla (died 940), who was minister to three Abbasid caliphs and was described as a prophet of calligraphy. Modern scholars are less sure; some argue that proportional rules existed before him. Even the basic numbers were contested. A 2020 study of the historical texts notes that writers never agreed on how many dots tall the alif should be.3 The calm of a beautifully written page rests on a geometry that its practitioners debated for centuries.

concepts.title: Girih: Medieval Tiles and Modern Mathematics
concepts.contentHtml:
The third great family is geometry: stars and polygons laced together by zigzag bands, known as girih. The usual assumption was that designers drew these patterns line by line with a straightedge and compass. In 2007 two physicists, Peter Lu of Harvard and Paul Steinhardt of Princeton, proposed something cleverer in the journal Science. By about 1200, they argued, designers had begun to think of girih as tilings of a small set of shapes, from pentagons to bow-ties, each decorated with lines.1 Fit the tiles together and the lines join up into the familiar stars. Pattern scrolls drawn by Islamic craftsmen show exactly such shapes, though no actual tiles have been found.

They also looked at the Darb-i Imam shrine in Isfahan, Iran, built in 1453. Its pattern is almost identical to a Penrose tiling, described by the British mathematical physicist Roger Penrose in 1973. Such patterns are quasi-periodic: they show five-fold and ten-fold symmetries and look regular, yet never repeat exactly, a property found in real metal alloys, the quasicrystals, in 1984. If they are right, Iranian craftsmen built a nearly perfect quasi-crystalline pattern five centuries before Western mathematics described one.2

Now the debate:

  • Lu himself thinks the designers were probably unaware of the mathematics; they wanted a pattern that could grow without repeating.3
  • The idea was said to have been anticipated by the crystallographer Emil Makovicky, which caused controversy over who got there first.
  • The paper was followed by what the journal Nature Materials called a rather cryptic spate of comments and clarifications, so the details are still argued over.

A parallel argument surrounds the Alhambra, the palace complex in Granada, Spain, often said to contain all 17 possible wallpaper symmetry groups. The first careful count, by Edith Müller in 1944, found twelve, and the mathematician Branko Grünbaum argued in 2006 that many later claims came from authors copying one another. His deeper point: "Groups of symmetry had no relevance to artists and artisans who decorated the Alhambra.4" To understand a pattern, think in terms its makers would have recognised.

title: The Emperor's Workshop: Mughal Painting
description: Akbar's giant Hamzanama, how a royal studio shared one picture, and the naturalism of Jahangir's painters

concepts.title: A Storybook the Size of a Window
concepts.contentHtml:
Say "Mughal miniature" and people picture something you could hold in one hand. The first great project of the Mughal painting studio breaks that picture. The emperor Akbar, who ruled from 1556 to 1605, commissioned an illustrated Hamzanama, the "Book of Hamza": wild tales of the hero Hamza and his companions battling unbelievers, witches, giants and dragons. These stories were traditionally performed aloud rather than read, and Akbar had a written Persian version made for his imperial volumes.

Each page is about 65 centimetres tall and 52 wide, more like a small window than a miniature. The painting is gouache, an opaque watercolour, on prepared cotton backed with paper; the text is written on paper on the back, and the layers were glued together. Contemporary sources say the work filled 12 or 14 volumes of 100 paintings each and took 15 years,1 probably about 1562 to 1577: some 1,400 paintings. Two Iranian masters, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, brought to India by Akbar's father, directed artists drawn from all over northern India.

Look up the V&A page in which Hamza, in an orange and gold robe on a black horse, cleaves a lion's head with his sword while an enemy sliced in half lies in the foreground. The upright format, high viewpoint and minute ornament of weapons and textiles come from Iranian painting; the lively naturalism of the animals and birds comes from Indian traditions. That fusion is the start of the Mughal style.

Fewer than 200 pages survive. The largest group, 60 folios, is in the MAK (Museum of Applied Arts) in Vienna, and the second largest, 28, is in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. In the winter of 1880–81 the V&A's buyer Caspar Purdon Clarke walked into a curiosity shop in Srinagar, Kashmir, and found large paintings, some of which had been used in the shop windows to keep out the winter frost.2 At some point, probably in the 19th century, someone rubbed out the faces of all the living beings on those pages.

concepts.title: Many Hands, One Picture
concepts.contentHtml:
A Mughal painting was rarely the work of one artist. The emperor's Ketabkhana, the "House of Books", was library and studio in one, where Hindu and Muslim artists from northern India worked with Iranian masters, calligraphers, bookbinders and illuminators. The paintings, in opaque watercolour and often gold on paper, record their own division of labour.

In 1896 the South Kensington Museum, today's V&A, bought an unbound manuscript of the Akbarnama, the history of Akbar's reign that the polymath Abu'l Fazl began writing in 1590. It has 116 paintings covering the years 1560 to 1577, and under each one a court librarian wrote in red ink who did what.1 One artist made the design (tarh), the composition. A second, presumably junior, did the work ('amal), filling the outline with colour. Sometimes a specialist portraitist painted the faces of the main characters. These little notes let art historians name the artists and follow their careers.

A new ingredient arrived from Europe. During his conquest of Gujarat in 1572–73 Akbar met Portuguese visitors from Goa, and he later asked for a religious mission. The first Jesuits reached his capital, Fatehpur, in 1580, and the Christian paintings in their chapel caused a sensation: Akbar brought his leading courtiers to see them, then sent for his artists. Prints brought by later missions were studied closely, and occasionally copied precisely, as in a Martyrdom of Saint Cecilia painted by an artist named Nini around 1600.

What the painters took was selective. Some Akbarnama scenes gain a sense of depth from European art, but the rules of scientific perspective were not followed.2 In Akbar's Triumphant Entry into Surat, painted by Farrukh Beg about 1590–95, one figure in the crowd, in blue clothes and a black hood and with blue eyes, stands for the Europeans Akbar had met. Mughal painting absorbed Indian, Iranian and European ideas and made something none of them had produced alone.

concepts.title: Jahangir's Eye: A Zebra, Portraits and Five Copies
concepts.contentHtml:
Akbar's son Jahangir, emperor from 1605, made the art of the book his great passion and shared his great-grandfather Babur's fascination with the natural world. Like Babur he wrote memoirs, but unlike Babur he ordered his leading artists to paint the events, people, birds and animals he described.

In 1621 a delegation brought him rare creatures, among them an African zebra, an animal he had never seen, which looked like a horse painted with stripes. "One might say the painter of fate, with a strange brush, had left it on the page of the world," he wrote. The painting of it, now in the V&A, carries a note in Jahangir's own spidery handwriting,1 saying that it was the work of Mansur, one of his two leading artists, and recording how and when the zebra came to court. An emperor acting as his own museum label is rare, precious evidence of who painted what.

Portraits reached a new level of likeness. The English ambassador Sir Thomas Roe showed Jahangir a treasured miniature portrait by the English painter Isaac Oliver, and would only lend it, not give it. A leading court artist was ordered to copy it, and when Roe was shown the original together with five identical versions, he had difficulty recognising his own.2 Single portraits also served as templates: a portrait of the courtier Mirza Ghazi reappears at exactly the same size in a group scene of Jahangir and his courtiers, filled in with different colours.

Where did this naturalism come from? The V&A notes that it is usually attributed to the artists' exposure to European portraits,3 and the Roe episode shows how keenly they studied them. Yet sharp observation of animals and birds was already a strength of the Indian painters of Akbar's Hamzanama decades earlier. So the story is not simply one of copying Europe: European examples met a naturalism that Indian painters already practised.

title: Feathers and Thread: Aztec and Inca Art
description: The last Aztec feather headdress and the debate over its return, and why Inca cloth outranked gold

concepts.title: The Last Feather Headdress
concepts.contentHtml:
In the Weltmuseum Wien, Vienna's museum of world cultures, stands one of the most extraordinary objects to survive from Aztec Mexico: a towering fan of feathers about 1.3 metres high and 1.75 metres wide. Hundreds of long, gleaming green tail feathers of the quetzal bird dominate it. Its feathers were originally arranged in four zones of emerald green, red, brown and blue, and it is studded with more than a thousand small gold plates. The materials list reads like an aviary: feathers of quetzal, cotinga, roseate spoonbill, squirrel cuckoo and kingfisher, on wood, fibres, paper, cotton and leather. Its frame is three delicate nets stiffened with thin wooden rods, and each long feather is sewn to the nets and attached to its neighbours.

Such headdresses were once widely used in Mesoamerica and were associated with rulers, gods and priests. This one, made in the early 16th century, is the only one left anywhere.1

Everyone calls it "Moctezuma's headdress", and here the popular story falls apart. After the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire in 1519–21, many objects were shipped to Europe and listed, but this headdress cannot be identified in any of those lists.2 It first appears in writing in 1596, in an inventory of the collections at Ambras Castle in Innsbruck, misleadingly described as a "Moorish hat" with gleaming green and golden feathers. Nobody knows how it got there. The museum says the name "Crown of Montezuma" was given in the 20th century without evidence and thinks it more likely belonged to a priest, and the Mexican historian Federico Navarrete says its association with Moctezuma came much later.3

Its later life shaped what you see. It was restored in 1878 with new feathers and golden elements and mounted flat, conserved again in 1992, and moved from Ambras to Vienna, where it was shown in the Natural History Museum before passing to today's Weltmuseum. The history topic on the pre-Columbian Americas covers the Aztec state; this lesson is about what its artists made.

concepts.title: Too Fragile to Travel? A Restitution Standoff
concepts.contentHtml:
Mexico has wanted the headdress back for a long time. The first request came in the 1860s from Maximilian, Mexico's Habsburg emperor, and campaigns resumed from the 1980s. In 2020 Mexico asked to borrow it for a 2021 exhibition marking 500 years since the fall of Tenochtitlan, offering Habsburg-era treasures in exchange, including the gilded carriage of Maximilian and Carlota. Austria said no, citing the object's fragility,1 and the refusal caused diplomatic tension.

The fragility argument rests on real science. From 2010 to 2012 Mexican and Austrian specialists studied and conserved the headdress together, in a project born of the wish to display it in Mexico. They found at least 170 breaks in its 374 long quetzal feathers,2 nets torn in many places, and metal ornaments that had damaged the feathers around them. When it was taken off its mount, nearly 2,000 feather fragments that had already broken off came to light. Because every feather is attached to its neighbours, a jolt to one moves the others. Both sides agreed on the maximum acceleration it could bear, and Mexico asked Professor Wassermann of the Vienna University of Technology to test whether a journey could stay below it. His conclusion: it was practically impossible to move it by lorry or aircraft, the standard ways of moving loans, without risking damage.3

So is the case closed? Not everyone thinks so:

  • Some experts dispute the assessment, and activists such as the Mexican dancer Xokonoschtletl Gómora keep campaigning for its return.
  • In October 2026 an Austrian presidential hopeful, Gunther Fehlinger-Jahn, pledged to return it, suggesting that ownership could pass to Mexico while it stays in Vienna until transport is safe. An Austrian president cannot decide restitution alone, and a law on returning colonial-era objects is still pending.

Notice the shape of the debate. One side argues from the object's body: it may not survive the trip. The other argues from history and meaning: it belongs to Mexico. Separating ownership from location is one way such deadlocks are being broken, as the Benin Bronzes will show.

concepts.title: Cloth Worth More Than Gold: Inca Textiles
concepts.contentHtml:
Travel south to the Andes and the ranking of materials changes again. In the ancient Andes, textiles, more than gold and precious stones, marked a person's social status,1 as the museum at Dumbarton Oaks puts it. Andean societies achieved political cohesion without written language, and cloth carried much of the load: it embodied wealth, signalled identity and, some scholars think, communicated complex ideas.

The finest Inca cloth, qompi (also spelled cumbi), was woven from cotton and camelid fibre, from llama, alpaca, guanaco and vicuña, by specialists and cloistered women, and reserved for the ruler and for rituals. Men's tunics, called uncu, were highly standardised in format, size and construction, made of interlocked tapestry, and like other Andean garments they were folded and stitched but never cut. The smoothest royal cloth felt so fine that the Spanish called it silk, a fabric Europe knew only from Chinese cloth.2

The weaving itself was state business. Qompi was woven on an unusual frame loom at least twice as wide as it was tall.3 Folded in the middle, the cloth became men's shirts, which the government handed out as uniforms or as rewards for service to the state. Spanish chroniclers described Inca soldiers in tunics like checkerboards, since such repeating designs marked social or military roles, while the most elaborate tunics carry small square designs called tocapu.

What do the tocapu mean? Nobody is sure. LACMA describes them as square geometric patterns associated with elite lineage, rank or profession. Others suggest the registered patterns may have worked as a still obscure system of communication,4 a kind of code in cloth. After the conquest the meanings faded: a double-sided tunic from the Lake Titicaca region, woven in the mid to late 16th century and now in the American Museum of Natural History in New York, almost a metre tall, keeps the Inca form and tocapu but adds silver metallic thread and different designs front and back, both European novelties.

title: Dreamings in Paint: Aboriginal Australian Art
description: Dating rock art with wasp nests, the Papunya painting movement of 1971, and the ethics of sacred designs

concepts.title: Dating a Kangaroo With Wasp Nests
concepts.contentHtml:
Aboriginal art has evolved from what is often called the world's oldest continuous art tradition. Proving the age of any particular rock painting, though, is fiendishly hard. Many are painted in ochre, an iron-oxide earth, and no current scientific method can tell when such paint was put on the rock.1 (The prehistory topic covers even older hand stencils from Indonesia.)

A team led by Damien Finch of the University of Melbourne found a clever way round the problem: mud wasps. In the Kimberley, in the north of Western Australia, wasps build mud nests on the walls and ceilings of rock shelters, and the nests contain tiny amounts of carbon that can be radiocarbon dated. A nest built on top of a painting must be younger than the paint, so it gives a minimum age. A nest the painting covers must be older, so it gives a maximum age.

Very rarely there are nests both under and over a single painting. That happened with a two-metre-long kangaroo painted in red-mulberry ochre across the sloping ceiling of a rock shelter above the Drysdale River, on Balanggarra Country. Three nests lay beneath it and three on top, which pinned its age to between 17,500 and 17,100 years, most likely about 17,300.2 Published in Nature Human Behaviour in 2021, it is Australia's oldest known rock painting still in place. Altogether 27 nest dates constrained 16 paintings in 8 shelters. They show that this early Naturalistic style, often life-sized animals in outline filled with irregular dashes, flourished from about 17,000 to 13,000 years ago, and that the later Gwion style of decorated human figures flourished around 12,000 years ago.

Notice how the science was done. Balanggarra Traditional Owners gave permission and supported the fieldwork, and at the request of the Balanggarra Traditional Owners, the published data do not give the exact locations of the sites.3 Protecting places and knowledge is a theme that runs through this whole lesson.

concepts.title: Papunya, 1971: Ceremony Moves to Board
concepts.contentHtml:
Papunya, about 250 kilometres west of Alice Springs, was a government settlement founded in 1960, to which Aranda, Anmatyerr, Luritja, Warlpiri and Pintupi people had been moved from their own lands. In 1971 a schoolteacher, Geoffrey Bardon, started a project to paint murals on a blank school wall. Men of the community took it up and painted a Honey Ant Dreaming mural, with Kaapa Tjampitjinpa and Johnny Warangkula Tjupurrula among them. Soon a group was painting in a Nissen hut, the Men's Painting Room, on anything to hand, from hardboard to floor tiles. Designs made for ceremony, in sand, on bodies and on sacred objects, were rendered permanent in synthetic polymer paint on composition board. As the National Gallery of Victoria puts it, artefact became art.1 The next year the artists named their company Papunya Tula, after two small hills that are a shared Honey Ant Dreaming site.

That is the classic story, and historians are complicating it. Kaapa Tjampitjinpa, an Anmatyerr man, was already painting on salvaged hardboard and selling work around the settlement. The patrol officer Jack Cooke entered several of Kaapa's boards in the 1971 Caltex Northern Territory Art Award; one was joint winner, and all seven works sold, earning him about $750 and causing a sensation back home.2 A reviewer citing the curator Luke Scholes argues that painting was already dynamic before Bardon arrived3 and that murals at a Warlpiri men's museum at Yuendumu inspired both Bardon and Kaapa. The movement was made by its artists.

The market followed, unevenly. In 1977 Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri painted Warlugulong. The Commonwealth Bank bought it that year for $1,200 and hung it in a staff training centre canteen for some 20 years.4 A Melbourne dealer bought it in 1996 for $36,000, and in 2007 the National Gallery of Australia bought it at a Sotheby's auction for $2.4 million. Visual artists then had no legal right to any share of such resale profits, and the case sharpened an Australian debate about a resale royalty for artists and their families.

concepts.title: Dots That Hide: Sacred Designs and Who May See Them
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is a belief worth testing: that dot painting is the ancient style of all Aboriginal art. It is not. Aboriginal art spans many regional languages of design. The Dharug and Dharawal artist Shane Smithers, who painted a 30-metre mural in Parramatta Square in Sydney, puts it bluntly: "We didn't have dots, we had lines.1" The rock engravings of his region show lines and figures, not dotted fields. Dots and concentric circles are associated with Western Desert art and spread across Australia after Papunya. Smithers points to road signs in New South Wales that, in his view, welcome drivers to local Country with iconography from somebody else's Country.

In the desert itself, dots were used long before 1971, in designs on bodies, on objects and on the ground. What changed is what they did. The first Papunya boards were startlingly explicit. In 1972–73 controversy erupted because founding artists had inadvertently included depictions of sacred objects2 (tjurunga) and ritual head ornaments in works taken into Alice Springs for sale. Such designs belong to men's ceremony and are restricted; many are not to be seen by women or uninitiated people.

The artists answered through style. The art historian John Kean says that as the paintings became more popular and travelled further, dots were used more often to obscure sacred and dangerous symbols.3 Johnny Warangkula Tjupurrula laid veils of white dots over the key elements of his Water Dreamings, softening what lay beneath; his layered dotting also evokes plants bursting up after rain. A dotted surface can be beautiful, meaningful and a screen all at once.

Museums now work within these rules. When the National Gallery of Victoria showed 200 of the first Papunya paintings in its exhibition Tjukurrtjanu, culturally sensitive works were hung separately after consultation and left out of the catalogue and website;4 when the show went to Paris, it had a restricted room at its heart. Knowing who may see a design is part of looking at this art properly.

title: The Benin Bronzes: Casting, Looting and Coming Home
description: What the Benin Bronzes are, how science traced their metal, and the arguments over who should hold them

concepts.title: Brass, Not Bronze: What the Benin Bronzes Are
concepts.contentHtml:
The so-called Benin Bronzes are thousands of heads, plaques, figures and other works made between the 16th and 19th centuries for the royal court of the Kingdom of Benin, in today's Edo State, Nigeria. The history topic on Africa's kingdoms tells the story of the kingdom and the British attack of 1897. Here the questions are what the objects are, how they were made and where they belong.

Start with the name, because it is wrong twice over. Many treasures in the group are carved ivory, not metal at all.1 And the metal ones are mostly not bronze.2 More than 700 chemical analyses show that the majority are brass (copper with zinc) or leaded brass, sometimes with a little tin. Earlier Nigerian castings from Igbo-Ukwu have a quite different make-up.

What were they for? Plaques showing historical scenes were displayed on the palace walls; the bent sides of one in the Cleveland Museum of Art show how it was fixed to wooden beams.3 Commemorative heads stood on ancestral altars for past Obas (kings) and Iyobas (queen mothers); a new Oba commissioned one for his predecessor's shrine. Each represents an individual, but the features are idealised, and the netted caps and necklaces echo real coral regalia. The title of Iyoba was first given in the late 1400s to4 Idia, mother of Oba Esigie; an Iyoba had her own palace and commanded her own regiment.

The makers were the Igun Eronmwon, the hereditary guild of metal casters, using the lost-wax method. A figure was modelled in wax; for plaques, moulds pressed out general shapes and details such as a warrior's staff were added by hand. Molten metal was then poured into a carefully made mould of wax and clay, and the metal took the place of the wax, which is lost in the process. Today's guild members still make works for royal and non-royal buyers, and the bronze caster Phil Omodamwen recently made a new plaque for the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford showing the looting of 1897; now bright gold, it will darken to the deep brown of the old ones. As he says, "The new will become old."

concepts.title: Tracing the Metal: Manillas and Lead Isotopes
concepts.contentHtml:
Benin's casters got their brass through trade. From the opening of the Portuguese trade in the late 15th century, hundreds of thousands of manillas, open horseshoe-shaped rings of copper and brass, were shipped from Europe to West Africa, and historians long suspected they were melted down for the bronzes. But earlier studies found no proof, partly because the manillas available for testing were later and too impure.

A 2023 study led by Tobias Skowronek, published in PLOS ONE, used lead isotopes. Lead comes in several isotopes whose ratios differ from one ore deposit to another, and the ratios do not change during smelting, so they act as a fingerprint of where metal was mined. Earlier work had found Benin Bronzes oddly uniform: of 212 analysed, 113 fall into an unusually small field of ratios.1 The team analysed 67 manillas, including early ones recovered from 16th- and 17th-century shipwrecks. The early manillas matched the Benin Bronzes, and both matched the lead-zinc ores of the German Rhineland, where brass was made between Cologne and Aachen using local calamine, a zinc ore. Later manillas matched only some of the bronzes.2 The study concludes that Rhineland manillas were probably the principal metal source, while noting that differences in trace elements mean they may not have been the only one.3 Their high lead content made an easy-flowing casting brass.

This science carries an uncomfortable history. As the Cleveland Museum of Art states, European manillas were exchanged for people whom the Edo had enslaved in wars.4 The metal of the plaques is entangled with the Atlantic slave trade.

Other detective work concerns display. The palace plaques were already in storage before 1897. An art historian has since reconstructed their former arrangement on the palace walls virtually, working from their dimensions and their imagery.5

concepts.title: Who Should Hold Them? The Restitution Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
After the 1897 attack at least 3,000 objects were scattered worldwide. The British Museum holds around 900 and is barred by a 1963 UK law from permanently removing items from its collection.1 Since 2022 others have moved:

  • Germany agreed in July 2022 to transfer ownership of more than 1,100 objects from five museums to Nigeria, with some left in Germany on loan. Foreign minister Annalena Baerbock said: "It was wrong to take the bronzes, and it was wrong to keep them for 120 years."
  • The Smithsonian in Washington deaccessioned 29 bronzes in October 2022; nine are back on display there on loan from the kingdom of Benin.
  • London's Horniman Museum transferred ownership of 72 objects in November 2022, sent six back and keeps the rest on loan.2

Then came a twist. In March 2023 a presidential declaration recognised the Oba, Ewuare II, as owner and custodian of the returned artefacts.3 Many Edo people saw that as right, since the objects were taken from his great-great-grandfather, but European museums dealing with Nigeria's national museums commission asked who their partner now was. Cambridge paused its return, then confirmed it. The new Museum of West African Art in Benin City stalled after protesters broke in at its planned opening.

The arguments, fairly put:

  • For return: the objects were seized in a violent attack; the Oba and the Nigerian government both claim them; and casters say that while the bronzes stay abroad, it is harder to inspire the next generation.
  • Against, or for caution: the Restitution Study Group, led by Deadria Farmer-Paellmann, a descendant of enslaved people taken from Benin, sued to stop the Smithsonian's return, arguing that the bronzes link Americans descended from enslaved people to their heritage. It lost, and the US Supreme Court declined to hear the case in 2024.4 Others ask whether the state or the Oba should own them, and where they can be kept and seen.

A common compromise has emerged: transfer the title, then lend some objects back. Ownership and location no longer have to be the same thing.
